tagline.text: Sorsogon's active volcano and the national park of lakes and forest around it

location.label: Location
location.text: Bulusan, Irosin and Juban, Sorsogon (Bulusan Volcano Natural Park)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–May dry season (always check the eruption alert level)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–4,000 (transport from Sorsogon City and meals, rough estimate for one day)

children.text: Bulusan is a stratovolcano in southern Sorsogon with frequent steam-driven eruptions. On November 18, 2026, it was at Alert Level 1, and entry within 4 km of the summit was prohibited. Visit the lake and forest only where the park has opened them to visitors.
Bulusan Volcano (Mount Bulusan) is a stratovolcano in Sorsogon in southeastern Luzon. According to Wikipedia it lies about
70km
southeast of Mayon Volcano and about
390km
southeast of Manila. It sits on the northeast rim of the Irosin caldera, which formed about 36,000 years ago, and its height is given variously as 1,565 m and 1,535 m, so think of it as around
. The base is about
15km

across. Around the mountain are towns such as Barcelona, Bulusan, Casiguran, Gubat, Irosin and Juban. A group of smaller volcanic edifices is also listed nearby, including Batuan, Binitacan, Calaunan, Calungalan, Homahan, Jormajan, Juban and Tabon-Tabon, so it is more accurate to see it as a volcanic zone of several peaks than as a single mountain.

The volcano is known less for magma eruptions than for phreatic eruptions, in which groundwater meets hot rock and explodes as steam and ash. Wikipedia says it has erupted 15 times since 2016 and is the fourth most active volcano in the Philippines after Mayon, Taal and Kanlaon. The June 5, 2022 eruption produced an ash column about 1 km high, and the April 28, 2025 eruption sent a plume about 4,500 m high over about 24 minutes, with a pyroclastic density current traveling up to about 3 km from the summit vent. Because of this history, Bulusan is less a place to go for the scenery than a place where you check the alert situation first. A little more of the record: in June 2006 an ash emission led to Alert Level 2, damaging houses in Casiguran and sending ash as far as Sorsogon City. On July 31, 2007 a steam and ash column rose about 5 km for 20 minutes, and in February 2011 water met hot magma and a plume about 2 km high rose, with thousands evacuated. There were also eruptions of about 2 km on June 10 and December 29, 2016, and on August 18, 2021 the alert was lowered from Level 1 to Level 0. That it can be quiet and then suddenly erupt is the key premise of any trip here.

The mountain's surroundings are designated Bulusan Volcano Natural Park. It became a national park by Proclamation No. 811 on June 7, 1935, was reclassified as a natural park by Proclamation No. 421 on November 27, 2000, and Wikipedia says it was declared a national park again by Republic Act No. 11038 (Expanded NIPAS Act), signed in July 2018, though other sources do not confirm this, so check the current classification locally. Sources differ slightly on the area (about 3,640 to 3,673 hectares); it is commonly given as about 3,672 hectares, and at its heart is Bulusan Lake, the place travelers visit most. See the separate Bulusan Lake entry for the lake area.

The forest is reported to hold birds such as the Philippine hawk-eagle, the flame-breasted fruit-dove and the Philippine eagle-owl, as well as lizards, frogs, bats and snakes. Deer, warty pigs and civets were once sighted, but it has not been confirmed that they still live there. This entry is not a summit-climbing guide; it is meant for understanding the volcano, for safety, and for sightseeing around it. Park entrance fees, trail openings and guide rules have too little documentation, so confirm directly with the Sorsogon tourism office.

A cone-shaped volcano about 1,550 m high, said to have four craters. The first is the Blackbird Lake crater, about 20 m across, and the fourth opened on the northeast rim during the 1981 eruption. Even just seen from a distance, the scale of the landform comes across. Its neighbors also include a group of other volcanic edifices.
The
4 km

radius around the summit is a permanent danger zone and is currently closed. PHIVOLCS also urges caution in the additional 2 km zone to the southeast. Leave summit climbing off the itinerary and ask the tourism office which lake and forest areas are open.
The park has two lakes, Bulusan Lake and Lake Aguingay. Lake Aguingay sometimes fills and dries up in summer. The forest paths around the lakes are the nature most travelers meet most easily.
Hot springs such as Mapaso, Masacrot, San Benon and San Vicente are known around the volcano. Hours and fees can change, so confirm locally.

blocks.title: A drive through the villages around the volcano

children.text: The road linking towns such as Bulusan, Irosin, Juban and Gubat is a drive where the volcano stays in view. Right after an eruption, roads can be blocked or covered in ash.
Philippine hawk-eagles, fruit-doves and owls are reported, and early morning is best. You will want binoculars and quiet footsteps.

blocks.title: How to read the alert levels

children.text: PHIVOLCS issues alerts on a scale from 0 to 5. The boundaries of danger zones and the extent of access restrictions may change with activity. On your travel day, follow the latest bulletin and local closures. An increase in volcanic earthquakes can raise the risk of sudden steam-driven eruptions even when the alert level stays the same.

items.title: A safe day
items.subtitle: Lake and villages, outside the danger zone

children.text: From your lodging in Sorsogon City, check the PHIVOLCS alert level and local guidance before setting out.
Head toward Bulusan Lake and walk the lake trail. See the Bulusan Lake entry for the lake.
Have lunch with local food in a nearby town.
Move toward Irosin and check whether the hot springs are open.
Return to Sorsogon City before dark.
Keep the summit and the 4 km permanent danger zone off this itinerary. Confirm on the day that the lake or forest trails are open, and switch to a Sorsogon City itinerary if access is restricted.

items.title: Southern Sorsogon, 2 days 1 night
items.subtitle: Volcano, lake and island beaches at Matnog

children.text: On the first day, visit Bulusan Volcano Natural Park and the lake.
Rest at the hot springs in Irosin.
On day two, go to Matnog and plan an island day at Subic Beach and Juag Lagoon.
Linking with the Matnog entry lets you see southern Sorsogon in one trip.
A flight from Manila to Legazpi is reported to take about
1 hour
. From Legazpi you take a bus or van toward Sorsogon and Irosin.
From Legazpi to Sorsogon City is reported to take about
1.5–2 hours
overland. Confirm fares and times locally.
Long-distance buses run from Manila toward Matnog and Sorsogon, reported to take about
12–14 hours
From Sorsogon or Irosin to the villages around the volcano you can use jeepneys, vans and tricycles.
See also the Sorsogon City entry.
Public transport around the volcano is sparse, and it is common to charter a vehicle.
If an eruption alert is in effect, roads may be controlled, so check local government announcements before you leave.

In volcano country the alert level takes priority over the weather. In the dry months of March–May roads are dry and many days are clear, which is good for walking around the lake and forest. In the rainy season, heavy rain can cause lahars or river flooding, so stay away from rivers and gullies.
Whatever the month, check the latest PHIVOLCS alert before you visit and ask the local tourism office which areas are open.

There are few lodgings around the volcano, so many visitors stay in Sorsogon City or near Irosin and visit as a day trip. Check rates and vacancies by date on a booking site. They can fill up in peak season and on holidays.

Meals are at restaurants in Sorsogon City, Irosin and Bulusan town. The Bicol region is known for dishes with coconut milk and chili, so if you are sensitive to spice, ask about the heat when ordering. Bring water and snacks before heading to the lake or forest.

Leave some slack in volcano-area travel. If the alert level suddenly rises, parts of the lake, forest and roads may close, so split your day in two so that you can swap in an alternative such as the hot springs or a town visit if one side is blocked. When booking lodging, it is reassuring to check the cancellation policy.
Check the PHIVOLCS alert level and local government announcements just before you visit.
The 4 km Permanent Danger Zone around the summit is off limits even at Alert Level 0. Stay within areas opened by park and local authorities.
Bring a mask and water. On days when ash is blowing, protect your eyes and airways.
Non-slip shoes are best on days you walk by the lake and forest.

The
PHIVOLCS bulletin

for November 18, 2026 reports Alert Level 1. Entry within the 4 km permanent danger zone is prohibited, and caution is required in the additional 2 km zone to the southeast. Check the latest bulletin and local restrictions on the day of travel.
Even at Level 0, rockfalls, landslides and sudden explosions are possible inside the danger zone.
Blowing ash is harmful to eyes and lungs, so wear a mask and protective glasses.
In the rainy season there is a risk of lahars and river flooding, so do not stay near rivers.
Farms and schools inside the danger zone may be evacuated or closed during an eruption, so local plans can change.
Park rules and trail openings are poorly documented, so confirm with the tourism office.
